extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in internet culture, online behaviour, and online harassment
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and characterize the phenomenon of internet trolling: definitions, types, motivations, effects, responses, legal/regulatory context, and community/technical aspects. Useful for readers seeking to identify or study trolling behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling is when a person posts deliberately offensive or provocative messages online (such as in social media, a forum, a chat room, an online video game) or performs similar behaviours in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messages can be inflammatory, insincere, digressive, extraneous, or off-topic, and may have the intent of provoking others into displaying emotional responses, or manipulating others' perceptions; behaviour is typically for the troll's amusement or to achieve results such as disrupting a rival's activities or causing confusion or harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application / subjectivity of the term
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the term 'troll' is subjective: some readers may characterise a post as trolling while others may regard the same post as a legitimate (even if controversial) contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More potent acts of trolling are blatant harassment or off-topic banter. The word is sometimes incorrectly used to refer to anyone with controversial or differing opinions — such use goes against the ordinary meaning of 'troll'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of trolling behaviour (content and intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling can be identified by offensive content intended to provoke an emotional reaction, off-topic or extraneous posts, insincere or digressive messages, or attempts to manipulate perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for deliberate provocation, repeated attempts to derail discussion, posting true information in misleading contexts, identity deception, hoaxes, or patterns of behaviour that prioritize eliciting reactions ('lulz') over genuine contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grades of trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: NetLingo (as cited) suggests four grades of trolling: playtime trolling, tactical trolling, strategic trolling, and domination trolling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grades distinguish light/inside-joke trolling from more organized, persistent, or harmful forms that aim for strategic or domination-level disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations of trolls
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivations range from benign amusement to sadistic pleasure, seeking 'lulz', desire to cause emotional responses, to achieving political/corporate goals (manipulation, disruption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding motive helps distinguish between humor/insider joking and malicious harassment or state-sponsored information operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling as identity deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling is often a game about identity deception: the troll attempts to pass as a legitimate participant, sharing the group's concerns while intending to deceive and provoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poster is genuinely participating or masquerading (sockpuppetry, false flags); groups may respond by distinguishing real from trolling postings and attempting to make the troll leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern trolls pretend to be sympathetic to a point of view while secretly ridiculing it; they declare interest or concern but subtly sow fear, uncertainty, and doubt within the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for posts that appear allied but consistently undercut or discourage effective action — e.g., 'I agree with your ends but not your means' — and examples include political deception used to influence group behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikipedia troll message design
rubrics_metrics.description: A Wikipedia troll supplies essentially true information but presents it in the wrong context, intending the audience to draw false conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design is 'tricky' because the information is accurate but framed to mislead; such trolls often provide no emotional input and instead spread misinformation via authoritative sources' appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sponsored, corporate, and special-interest trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and countries may employ trolls to manipulate public opinion (astroturfing), sometimes called state-sponsored Internet propaganda or 'sockpuppet armies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Chinese '50 Cent Party' and coordinated campaigns; evaluate scale, timing (e.g., around holidays), and organizational patterns rather than lone-person behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Troll sites and hotspots
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain online spaces (e.g., 4chan, /b/ board, Encyclopedia Dramatica, TOTSE, some anonymous message boards) are recognised as centres for trolling activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such spaces often enable anonymity, rapid posting, and cultures that reward provocative harassment; these sites can be bases to target other platforms and users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological characteristics linked to trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Research correlates trolling behaviour positively with sadism, trait psychopathy, Machiavellianism (dark triad/tetrad), and anti-social tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies suggest trolls take pleasure from causing pain and emotional suffering; gender differences (men more likely) and personality predictors (sadism, psychopathy) can inform risk assessment but are not deterministic diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and deindividuation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity of online postings can lead to disinhibition and increased incidence of flaming and trolling; anonymity allows behaviours unlikely in public or professional settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms that reduce anonymity (registration, verified identities) may increase accountability and reduce some trolling, though other factors (culture, moderation) also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community effects and harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling can disrupt discussions, disseminate bad advice, damage trust in online communities, and emotionally harm targets; high rates of deception can cause groups to dismiss genuine newcomers as trolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include chilling effects on participation, reputational damage, and increased moderation burden; awareness of these harms should guide community policies and moderation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses and moderation strategy: 'Don't feed the trolls'
rubrics_metrics.description: A common strategy is to ignore rather than engage with trolls — 'please don't feed the trolls' — on the idea that trolls feed on attention and reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychologists consider withholding attention as often the best way to stop trolling; moderators may combine ignoring with bans, registration requirements, or active removal. Beware of 'extinction burst' where disruption may increase briefly after contact ceases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and regulatory context
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal treatment of trolling varies by jurisdiction; trolling per se is not a federal crime in the U.S., while other countries (e.g., UK, Japan) have statutes that can criminalise certain online insults or communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: UK Malicious Communications Act 1988 and Communications Act 2003; Japan's 2022 ban on 'online insults'; enforcement and sentencing vary. Cyberbullying laws differ by state/country; legal remedies depend on local statutes and case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling as a subculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling has developed its own rituals, rules, specialised language, and dedicated spaces; some trolls self-identify and perform for a nameless audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise trolling's cultural markers (memes, jargon like 'Trollface', 'lulz') when assessing whether behaviour is subcultural joking versus targeted harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics, techniques and examples of trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tactics include hoaxes (fake 'Gold Membership'), impersonation, posting inflammatory comments on memorial pages, fake news/false flags, posting true information out of context, and creating fake accounts or scams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article include hoaxes that fooled mainstream media (e.g., Jenkem), organized harassment of memorial pages, and fabrication campaigns used in political contexts; detection looks for coordinated timing, account networks, and framing manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and mitigation challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring trolling is difficult while maintaining freedom of speech; technical detection (bots/cyborgs) and moderation face limits and require trade-offs between openness and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms may require registration, use human review plus technology, publish archives of state-backed operations, or employ community moderation; training in critical thinking is recommended to reduce gullibility to manipulative trolling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of meaning and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling evolved from early inside-joke/novice baiting on Usenet (gentle practice) to a broader modern sense encompassing harassment, information warfare, and political activism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding historical usage helps distinguish 'playful' veteran-user trolling from modern harmful forms; early forms sometimes functioned as group-identification rather than malicious conduct.
